_README: Every human judgement about this ROM lives in this file; the
generated listings are disposable, so renaming is free.
What to do next, roughly in order:
Read the coverage it reports. Low coverage is normal at
first and is the number you are trying to move.
2. Every unresolved indirect jump it reports is a hole. Add the
target to `entries`, or the pointer pair to `ram_vectors` if
the handler is installed into RAM.
Finds the sound code and the tables feeding it.
4. Name things in `labels` as soon as you know what they are.
See docs/method.md for the working order and docs/pitfalls.md for
the traps that each cost real time.

headers.rom:B572: Copies the RAM POKEY shadow ($2113-$211D, one freq/ctrl pair per channel) out to hardware. The values it copies are computed just above from live game state (paddle position, ball distance -- shifts and compares, then ORA #$C0/#$A0 to set POKEY's distortion bits), not read from a note table. Called from $B31A and $B350. This is a *separate* engine from the composed theme (see LoadThemeSong/NoteTable) -- real-time generative audio driven by gameplay, most likely the in-match sound effects/adaptive layer rather than the attract-mode theme.
headers.rom:FDB7: Display-list interrupt for the scrolling grid. WSYNC-timed writes to P0C2/P0C3 make the horizon colour gradient; the same handler also drives a rising/falling siren by adding dat_FE4E's per-channel deltas into AUDF1-4 (via DliVolumeSweep at $FE32) once per call, gated by the TaskVecLo/Hi countdown. Installed into DliVecLo/Hi at $FC35.
headers.rom:B1F4: Sets SongPtrLo/Hi = $B6D2 (the theme's note-event stream) and SongDoneVecLo/Hi = $B15E (a section/loop dispatch table). Reached from InitPokeySilence's boot chain via sub_B11D <- sub_98C0 <- RESET, so this fires once at power-on -- matches the theme starting immediately at boot, before any input. sub_B11D is also called from $9A86 and $BC60, which are worth checking as the 'plays again at the end' restart points.
headers.rom:B219: ThemeSongTick: reads one event from (SongPtrLo/Hi),Y. A $00 byte ends the stream and jumps through SongDoneVecLo/Hi ($B15E) rather than falling off the end -- that's the loop-back to the top of the theme, or a section change. Otherwise the byte is a duration (kept in ram_2107, and only when it counts down to zero does a new event get read -- see the DEC ram_2107/BEQ at $B23B, so duration really does mean 'hold this note N ticks'). The following byte is checked by its sign (BPL at $B25F): if positive it indexes NoteTable (index*3) as documented; if negative -- CONFIRMED, this includes $FF -- the table lookup is skipped entirely and the corresponding channel's frequency shadow byte is set straight to $00, i.e. silence. So a negative note-index byte is a rest, not a held note; that was confirmed from the branch logic itself, no live capture needed. Called once per invocation from DliHandler_GridMusic ($E213) -- NOT a round-robin task slot (that was wrong in an earlier note); it's a display-list-interrupt handler, one link in a chain (see rom:E213). Ticks forward by one event each time that DLI fires.
headers.rom:B5CD: Three parallel arrays (dat_B5CD/B5CE/B5CF), indexed by note*3 from ThemeSongTick: divider byte, distortion+volume byte (POKEY AUDC-shaped -- high nibble distortion, low nibble volume), and a third byte that's usually $00. ~70 entries, B5CF running to B6A2.
headers.rom:B6D2: The theme song itself: a stream of (duration, note-index) byte pairs read by ThemeSongTick, 603 bytes, terminated by a single $00 at $B92C. CONFIRMED: $FF (and any note-index byte with bit 7 set) is a rest -- ThemeSongTick's sign check on this byte skips the NoteTable lookup and zeroes that channel's shadow byte instead of looking up a pitch (see rom:B219). A phrase around $B6E2-$B722 repeats almost verbatim later in the stream -- consistent with an audibly looping riff.
headers.rom:DCBE: DistanceToBall, called per-player (X = 0 or 1) from VEC_997C. Computes dx = ballX - playerX[X] and dy = ballY - playerY[X] as signed 16-bit subtractions (low byte at $008B/$008E vs $008D/$0090 for X, $00A6/$00A9 vs $00A8/$00AB for Y), then takes the absolute value of each (EOR #$FF / ADC #1 when negative) into ram_004E/ram_0051. The magnitude is then compared against #$02 and #$04, tail-jumping into sub_DD8A/sub_DDE7 -- code shared with the graphics engine (see the retraction on rom:DE2A), so what this specific call path uses the result for is still open. ram_22E8/dat_9A4C (an earlier candidate for the real facing driver) was tested and found too sparse -- see rom:D19C for what was actually confirmed.
headers.rom:DE2A: 10 near-linear steps ($00,$1F,$3B,$57,$73,$8F,$AB,$C7,$E3,$FF -- roughly +28 each), read by sub_DDE7/L_DDE8. RETRACTED: an earlier note here guessed this was the 'Rotosnap' auto-facing threshold table. Disproved by a live capture (playback of Ballblazer/run-01.inp with a write-tap + screenshot on every change to ram_23B7, the cell this chain's caller touches): the counter cycled continuously from the very first frames of the Atari/Lucasfilm boot logos, before any Rotofoil exists on screen, so it can't be a facing indicator. Tracing the actual callers of sub_DDE7 (L_DDE8's containing routine) shows they're all in the graphics block $E703-$E9FC, the same block as DrawGridScanlines -- so this chain feeds the perspective floor's geometry, not ship rotation. sub_DD8A/sub_DDE7 are also reached as a tail of DistanceToBall, so the two subsystems share this utility rather than DistanceToBall owning it. What it actually computes for the floor isn't pinned down yet.
headers.rom:DE34: Permutation table read at dat_DE2A's bucket index, then reduced mod 8 (AND #$07). See the retraction on rom:DE2A -- this is shared/graphics-side, not a confirmed facing-direction table.
headers.rom:DE45: Copies several fixed blocks (dat_DEA9, dat_DF1A, dat_DED5, and others) from ROM into the live MARIA display-list RAM ($26xx-$27xx) once at boot. This is the *static template* -- the zone headers and starting graphics pointers -- that the per-frame code then edits in place. The live list was captured directly off a running MAME session with probes/dumpdl.lua + tools/dlwalk.py: 25 zones, $23BC-$2407, decoded in dlwalk-output.txt alongside this doc.
headers.rom:8020: RETRACTED 'ship/UI sprite art' identification, corrected to floor tiles. An earlier pass rendered $8020/$8038/$8085/$809D/$881F/$8837/$8875/$888D with gfx.py's indirect-mode grid at a large --lines value (128, the tool's default) and reported ship shapes, the 'ballblazer' logo, and HUMAN/DROID menu text. That was a tooling artifact -- these are direct-mode entries, only 21-27 bytes wide by the zone's real 8 lines tall, and the indirect-mode grid at 128 lines reads 120 extra unrelated pages per column, picking up whatever else happens to share that low byte far beyond the object's real extent. Re-rendered correctly (gfx.py --direct WIDTH --lines 8, added this session because of this mistake): $8020 and $8085 are solid two-tone fills (constant $AA/$55 bytes on every line -- the flat-coloured wall/sky bands visible above and below the chequerboard floor in every screenshot); the other six ($8038, $809D, $881F, $8837, $8875, $888D) are all small anti-aliased diagonal-edge tiles, confirmed against the live display list's paired RAM graphics pointer too (e.g. $18A8, dumped from ramdump.bin, shows the identical diagonal pattern shifting frame to frame) -- this is the chequerboard floor's own edge-smoothing tileset, the same subsystem as DrawGridScanlines/AdvanceRowColorPhase, not ship or UI art. Where the real ship sprite lives is open -- see the retraction on rom:9800 for the closest lead (small diagonal-wedge fragments used during the match-end spin, possibly assembled from several tiles rather than one dedicated sprite). FOLLOW-UP: a dedicated search (live DL capture during ordinary play at a screenshot-confirmed frame showing the ship, ramdump-ship.bin) ruled out several explanations with evidence rather than finding it: not a missed dlwalk.py entry (its zone terminator logic was verified directly against the raw bytes -- the trailing bytes after each zone's real entries are stale RAM, not a missed third entry); not a second display list (DPPH/DPPL had zero writes across the whole frame); not present in any of the 25 zones' actual graphics entries (all enumerated: empty zones, confirmed floor tiles at new scroll-phase addresses, the HUD font, and three small unidentified palette-4 objects in zones 20-22 that screen-position reasoning suggests are more likely the ball than the ship); not written by any unaccounted-for code (a live write-tap on the whole display-list entry region during 400 frames of active play found 281 distinct writer addresses, all already mapped to the floor/perspective engine -- no new writer stood out the way the spin's fragment selector did with the same technique). RESOLVED (later pass, see rom:BD80): none of those explanations were it. The ship isn't a display-list entry at all in the sense this search was looking for -- it's assembled fresh into the live list every frame from the diagonal-wedge fragment sheet at $9800-$AFFF, distance-scaled via the $9000-96FF table (sub_BD80) and placed via the same rotation-phase dispatcher already traced for the match-end spin (RotationPhaseToFragment/PickSpinFragment). At long range it's rendered as one of the small 4px palette-4 dots in zones 20-22 instead; the switch to the fragment-assembled silhouette is a live, confirmed distance-based level-of-detail transition (screenshots: docs/img/ship-lod-*.png).
headers.rom:BD80:
sub_BD80 -- SHIP FOUND. This is the second confirmed reader of the $9000-96FF reciprocal/perspective table (the first is sub_F89D, the floor engine -- see rom:9000), and tracing it live resolves the long-open 'where is the real ship' question. Called four times (X = per-player index) from L_E2EC/L_E314/L_E3AE/L_E3D6, all inside DliHandler_GridMusic's per-zone dispatcher (rom:E213) -- i.e. every frame, not spin-only. Sets a fixed base position ($0063/$0064 = $80/$50), loads per-player position deltas (ram_2375,X/ram_2378,X -- adjacent to ram_2376/2379, part of the SteerTowardTarget/BallOrbitPhysics position-array cluster, see rom:D1DA for what those turned out to actually hold), then branches on a distance value (ram_235A,X, compared against #$08): distance 0 hardcodes the table's own first byte ($E7, i.e. 'as close/large as the table gets'); distance <8 reads the table directly at page ($8F+distance) offset ram_2357,X; distance >=8 reads it via a rotate-into-carry scaled index. The result feeds ram_231C, which is threaded (via ram_2329/232A/232B/232C) straight into the SAME dispatcher that reads PossessionState/ContestFlag (rom:E372's already-documented tail) to choose a fragment id and poke it into the live display list (PokeDisplayListByte, rom:CEDE). So the table supplies the DISTANCE-TO-SCALE/PLACEMENT term for whichever fragment gets drawn.

CONFIRMED LIVE (run-01.inp, ordinary play, frames 1-4000, no match end anywhere near this window): a write-tap on the exact instruction inside PokeDisplayListByte (PC=$CEEC / its sibling call site PC=$CE18) is SILENT from frame 1 through frame 2912, then starts firing every 1-2 frames from frame 2913 onward, writing fragment-sheet page bytes ($9E, $A0, $AA -- all inside the already-catalogued $9800-$AFFF fragment region, docs/sprites.html's 'spin-frag' category) into live corridor zone entries ($25A2, $2584). Screenshots taken across this exact window (docs/img/ship-lod-*.png) show why: at frame 2895 the opponent is a single-pixel dot near the horizon (the tiny 4px-wide palette-4 'unident' objects catalogued in the gallery, e.g. $989E/$9AA2/$A2A2 -- so those are a distant-LOD ship/goal marker, not confirmed as the ball as earlier guessed); by frame 2913, the exact frame the fragment-poke starts, it's a slightly larger 2-colour block; by frame 3600 it has grown into a full multi-tone triangular Rotofoil silhouette assembled from several fragments with two different palettes. This is a distance-based level-of-detail switch: far away the opponent is one small direct-mode dot, and once close enough the SAME fragment/perspective machinery already traced for the match-end spin (RotationPhaseToFragment/PickSpinFragment, rom:E372/rom:CEC1) engages continuously to assemble a bigger, shaped silhouette from the diagonal-wedge sheet, scaled/placed using this table. The match-end spin (rom:9800/rom:97EE) is the same renderer forced to cycle RotationPhase at maximum speed, not a separate system -- confirms the working theory already noted there. RETRACTS the framing of $9800-$AFFF as a 'match-end spin fragment sheet': it's the ship's general-purpose close-range rendering set, of which the spin is only the fastest-cycling special case.

FOLLOW-UP: sub_BD80 is not ship-exclusive either. Its X input is not always a per-player index -- a live read-tap on this routine's own instructions caught it firing with X values of 6, 7, 12 and 13 as well, which are goalpost slot numbers (see rom:9DD0/rom:9E7A), not player indices. Tracing the callers (sub_E378, rom:E378, the same dispatcher tail documented on rom:E372) shows a lookup (dat_E422/dat_E424, {6,18} and {12,24}, indexed by player and a facing/position boundary check) choosing which goalpost slot to feed sub_BD80 on a given call, alternating with the player-index calls across the dispatcher's four call sites. So this is a general-purpose 'distance to screen scale/position' utility built once around the $9000-96FF table and reused for both the opponent ship's fragment placement and the two goalposts' on-screen scale -- not two separate systems.

FOLLOW-UP: an earlier version of this note claimed the ball doesn't go through any display-list object at all, based on a genuine on-screen dot that turned out to be a video:snapshot()/-video none artifact -- CORRECTED, see FINDINGS.md item 14. The real answer, found afterward from a trustworthy screenshot (scr:pixel(), taken deliberately right before a goal on the strength of a direct user tip: 'the match timer freezes when a goal is scored, shortly before that the ball should be visible on at least one half of the screen'): the ball DOES render as a real, large, multi-zone object at close range -- it just uses a THIRD system, not this one. sub_BD80 IS involved (confirmed live: PC-tagged writes to ram_232B/232C immediately after 'JSR sub_BD80' at $E2EC show real, changing distance-scale values, not the $FF/$00 not-visible sentinel), called here with X alternating between 1 and 2 every frame (LDX #$01 on odd ram_0042 parity, else X=2) -- these are SLOT numbers into the SteerTowardTarget-adjacent position-delta arrays this routine reads (ram_2375,X etc.), not raw entity indices, and slots 1/2 are already confirmed (rom:9DB7) as 'player0 vs ball' and 'ball vs player1' -- i.e. this alternates which player's-eye-view of the ball gets updated each frame, but is BALL data both times, never the opponent ship (that's the separate fragment/silhouette system above). See rom:BF35 for what actually places it in the display list from there.
headers.rom:BF35: sub_BF35 -- BALL FOUND. The ball's own dedicated close-range placement routine, a THIRD system alongside the ship's wedge-fragment engine (rom:CEC1/rom:E372) and the goalpost's multi-zone placement (rom:C0DD) -- distinct code, though it reuses sub_BD80's PerspectiveTable-based distance math as an input. Gated by 'LDA ram_2026 / AND #$07 / BNE (return)' -- the exact same 'match actively running' gate already confirmed for SteerTowardTarget (rom:D1DA), so the ball is only placed here during live play, never pre/post-match. Reads ram_232B/232C, which the caller (rom:E372's dispatcher, at $E2EC/E2EF-E2F8) fills straight from sub_BD80's own ram_231B/231C output when called with X=1 or X=2 -- CONFIRMED LIVE these are real, changing values (not the '$FF/$00 -- not visible this frame' sentinel the same dispatcher falls back to otherwise), via a write-tap on ram_232B/232C during a goal approach (run-03.inp, frames 3295-3298). If ram_232B is negative (BMI), returns without drawing (off-screen/behind). Otherwise indexes three small ROM tables (dat_C043, dat_C054, dat_C03D/dat_C059 -- the last pair shared with the generic zone-builder cluster, rom:C677) to compute an X-screen-position and a graphics page per zone, spanning up to 4 zones (one call per zone, incrementing X each time, looping while a running distance total stays under the object's computed extent), and writes two 4-byte entries per zone via sub_C1D4/sub_C1E8 (the same generic 'write one poked object into (ram_0058),Y' pair the goalpost and floor-builder code also uses). CONFIRMED LIVE end to end (run-03.inp, first real in-match goal, frame 3307): a trustworthy screenshot (scr:pixel(), not video:snapshot() -- see the retraction on rom:BD80 and docs/pitfalls.md in the toolkit for why that distinction matters) at frame 3298 shows a large, unambiguous orange ball on screen, 9 frames before the goal, exactly matching a user-supplied gameplay tip ('the match timer freezes when a goal is scored, shortly before that the ball should be visible on at least one half of the screen') used to find this window in the first place. dlwalk decoded the live display list at that exact frame: zones 18-21 each hold a 2-entry, palette-4, width-2 object pair (e.g. $2692: gfx=$B083, x=85; $2696: gfx=$B085, x=91), and a direct write-tap on those exact zone bytes traced the writer straight to sub_C1D4/sub_C1E8's instructions, called from inside this routine. The MatchTimer-freeze half of the tip is also confirmed, though only at the byte/screen level so far, not yet traced to a specific instruction: at this same goal (frame 3307), the raw MatchTimerLo/Hi bytes (ram_23B3/ram_23B5) keep incrementing every single frame with no interruption, but the DISPLAYED HUD clock digits hold constant ('2:47.4') for at least 13 frames afterward (3307-3320, confirmed via trustworthy scr:pixel() screenshots, not the raw counter) -- so the freeze is real but lives in the HUD-digit-formatting/redraw step, not the underlying timer, which doesn't pause. RESOLVED, same day: see the fourth addition on rom:9B36 and rom:D520 for the full staged sequence -- ram_2026 bit 7 (the same 'match running' flag this routine's own gate reads) is what freezes it, cleared by sub_D520 at the moment of the goal and not restored until a full post-goal reset sequence completes several hundred frames later, which is also why sub_BF35 itself stops running for that same window.
headers.rom:C0DD: sub_C0DD -- the goalpost's own multi-zone placement routine, structurally the counterpart of rom:BF35 for the ball: takes a distance/position pair in ram_232D/232E (NOT computed here -- staged by the caller from sub_BD80's own output, see below), and writes a 2-entry object into each of several zones via the same sub_C1D4/sub_C1E8 generic writer, looping while ram_2318 (a computed span) isn't exceeded. CONFIRMED LIVE (run-03.inp, frame 3298, the goal-approach window also used for rom:BF35): a read-tap on its own entry instruction ('LDA ram_232D', PC=$C0DD) shows it called two or three times per frame, fed by two different callers -- $E28A and $E29B, inside the SAME dispatcher tail as rom:BF35 and rom:BD80's goalpost-slot calls (L_E3AE/L_E3D6, which call sub_BD80 with the goalpost SLOT values already confirmed on rom:BD80's first FOLLOW-UP, then stage the result through ram_232F/2330 and ram_2331/2332 for these two sub_C0DD calls to consume next). A direct write-tap on the resulting zone bytes (zones 21-24 in this capture) confirmed the graphics pages written are all in the $88CD/$84CD/$8CCD family, palette 2 -- distinct from the ball's palette-4 $B0xx/$A8xx/$A7xx/$9Fxx family from rom:BF35's zones -- matching the two purple goalpost pylons visible in the same screenshot. So the picture is now complete for all three close-range object types: the ship uses PickSpinFragment's single-zone wedge-silhouette assembly (rom:CEC1/rom:E372); the goalpost and the ball both use a materially different multi-zone 'wide object' placement style (this routine and rom:BF35 respectively), sharing sub_BD80's distance math and the sub_C1D4/sub_C1E8 zone-entry writer, but running as separate code with separate ROM graphics.
headers.rom:D520: sub_D520 -- GOAL DETECTOR FOUND. The ball-vs-goalpost collision check that actually registers a score, closing the front end of the pipeline sub_9B36 (the score arithmetic) sits at the back of. Compares the ball's position (ram_008D/0090, already confirmed as the ball's X pair) against ram_0094/0097 and ram_0095/0098 -- the entity-9 and entity-9+9=18 position slots sub_9D23 seeds, i.e. the two goalpost representations (rom:9DD0/rom:9CF5) -- plus a Y-range gate on ram_00A5/00A8/00AB against a fixed offset from #$1B (the same '27' boundary constant sub_9E7A's near/far selection and this routine's own Y-check both use). If the ball is outside either check, falls through to L_D562 -- CORRECTED, this is NOT a no-score return: it resets three scratch cells and jumps to sub_D5C0, leading into a SECOND, symmetric check (L_D571-L_D5A4) against a different entity pair (ram_009D/00A0 vs ram_009E/00A1) that sets ram_22C0 the same way but ORs bit 4 into ram_2026 instead of bit 5 -- the far-goalpost counterpart to this routine's near-goalpost check (matching the already-confirmed near/far dual representation, rom:9E7A), which is exactly why sub_9B36 clears both bits 4 and 5 (AND #$CF) rather than just one. The true entry point sits even further back, at L_D4E1 (rom:D4E1-area) -- itself gated on 'BIT ram_2026 / BMI (continue) / RTS', i.e. bit 7, the SAME match-running flag this whole detector's own output ends up clearing -- so goal detection itself pauses during the post-goal freeze window, and a second ball-position band (L_D503, not traced this pass) selects between this routine and a further variant before reaching either goalpost check. If inside either goalpost's bounds: bands a distance value (ram_00AA) against #$03 and #$10 into X=1, 2 or 3, storing it into ram_22C0 -- CONFIRMED LIVE this is exactly the 'goal increment' sub_9B36 adds into the score, previously documented there only as an input, its own origin untraced until now, so a goal's point value depends on precisely how close to the goalpost's centre the ball was when it crossed, not a flat 1 point per goal. Then, in one instruction sequence ('LDA ram_2026 / ORA #$20 / AND #$7F'), sets bit 5 and clears bit 7 in a single write -- CONFIRMED LIVE (run-03.inp, first real goal, frame 3305, one frame before sub_9B36 picks it up) this is the actual origin of the HUD-timer-freeze mechanism documented on rom:9B36's fourth addition below: clearing bit 7 here is what stops sub_982D (the HUD digit writer) and sub_BF35 (the ball's own renderer) from running at all, both gated on that same bit.
headers.rom:FE4A: dat_FE4A -- only 4 bytes ($56,$7F,$00,$2A), immediately followed by dat_FE4E (7 bytes, confirmed DliHandler_Grid siren-sweep deltas). Read together as a 10-byte block by the boot sequence's copy loop at $FC51 -- see rom:FC43 for the full resolution: only the first two bytes are individually meaningful (TaskVecLo/TaskVecHi countdown seeds), the rest are dat_FE4E's own data caught in the same bulk copy because it immediately follows in ROM, not a deliberately-authored 10-byte structure.
headers.rom:9000: 1792 bytes ($9000-$96FF, exactly 7 pages), found unmapped by the byte-coverage pass built for docs/sprites.html -- the single largest gap in the ROM (all other unmapped runs are under 270 bytes). CONFIRMED not graphics, checked exhaustively rather than by eye: every one of the 1792 byte-to-byte steps is non-increasing (255/255 decreasing steps on each of the 7 pages, 0 increasing anywhere), and the pages join continuously end-to-start ($90FF=$63, $9100=$63; $91FF=$37, $9200=$37; and so on through $9600=$00) -- one smooth monotonic curve from $E7 down to $00 across all 1792 samples. Real pixel art doesn't do this even by accident; shape is consistent with a reciprocal or perspective-divide table. CONFIRMED LIVE with a read-tap (PC-tagged, run-01.inp) that it has exactly two readers, both real 6502 code, both using genuine line-planar (ptr),Y addressing with the high byte stepping $90->$96: sub_F89D ($F89D-$F998, called from DliHandler_GridMusic's dispatcher every frame) feeds the floor engine's per-scanline edge array (ram_2260, read directly by DrawGridScanlines at $E73D) -- so it IS the perspective-divide table the floor needs, as guessed; and sub_BD80 ($BD80, see its own entry) uses the same table, indexed by per-player distance, to scale/place the opponent ship -- see rom:BD80 for the full resolution of where the ship actually lives. The preceding gap, $8FBC-$8FFB (64 bytes, irregular then zero-padded), is separate -- see rom:8FBC.
headers.rom:8FBC: 64-byte gap immediately before the $9000-96FF math table (rom:9000). Not zero throughout: $8FBC-$8FBF are zero, then 24 irregular bytes ($8FC0-$8FD7: F3,CF,3C,F0,3C,FF,CC,3C,2A,AA,AA,AA,80,AA,AA,AA,AA,A0,FC,0F,FC,FF,CF,3F), then zero-padded through $8FFB. Decoded as 2bpp direct-mode pixels (the format the confirmed neighbouring floor-edge tiles at $8020-$888D use), it does NOT look like hand-drawn art: no smooth antialiasing gradient, just a dithered 0/3 run, then 17 flat pixels of index 2 (from a literal run of $AA bytes -- 10101010, a common filler/padding value, not a drawn shape), then dithering again -- structurally a padding pattern, not a tile. CONFIRMED LIVE the suspicion is right: a PC-tagged read-tap on the full $8FBC-$8FFB range across the whole of run-03.inp (18650 frames) logged 92650 raw hits, but every single distinct PC checked resolves to either a RAM-operand instruction (SBC ram_00A9,X at $9DDB, SBC ram_0052,X at $9E24, STA ram_00C4,Y at $D2B3, ADC ram_22FC at $ED0E, SBC ram_21FD,Y at $F408, LDA ram_2230,X at $E74F -- the last one is DrawGridScanlines itself, the floor engine, which explains the huge per-frame count) or a no-operand instruction (ROL A at $D423, CLC at $F40F/$F433) -- none of them reference this ROM range at all. The first 12 bytes are even attributed to PC=$2404, which is a RAM address and cannot be a real 6502 program counter. Same shared-bus misattribution artifact already identified and closed for the dead slots 24/25 (rom:9EBB): MARIA's own graphics DMA is very active reading ROM during ordinary play (25 zones, several empty and probed every frame) and the emulator's tap stamps those hardware bus cycles with whatever the CPU's PC register happens to hold at that instant, not a real fetch from this address. CLOSED: genuinely unused ROM space -- most likely alignment padding ahead of the $9000-aligned math table, not an asset or a missed reader.
headers.rom:E213: DliHandler_GridMusic. Entered via DliVecLo/Hi (JMP (DliVecLo) inside ENTRY_Nmi) -- confirmed by the code just above it at $E1F9 arming the *next* DLI's address before RTI, and this handler doing the same (arms $E42C) after its own work. So this is one link in a rotating chain of per-zone DLI handlers, not a round-robin task-table slot. Calls DrawGridScanlines ($E74A) to race the beam for this zone's scanlines, then ticks ThemeSongTick once. Found by tapping every write to $2300-$27FF live (probes/watch-dl-pc.lua) and reading the CPU's PC at each write -- the direct way to find a writer when static tracing alone doesn't reach it.
headers.rom:E74A: DrawGridScanlines. A chain of near-identical 8-scanline loops (starting near $E97A, through sub_E9A5/E9C2/E9DF/E9FC/EA19/EA36, ending with the single-line sub_EA51). Each loop reads two per-row source tables 8 bytes apart -- one at ram_2230+8n (the 'edge' family: 2230,2238,2240,2248,2250,2258...) giving this row's boundary value, which it also propagates (+$60) into the *next* zone's edge pair (e.g. ram_24B5/24B9) -- and one at ram_2291+8n (the 'colour phase' family: 2291,2299,22A1,22A9,22B1,22B9...) used to index ColorCycleSuccessor for the actual byte. Every scanline: STA WSYNC, then STX P0C1 / STA P0C2. This is the render stage of the corridor -- a classic 'racing the beam' perspective floor built from per-scanline playfield-colour writes, not sprite scaling. What it draws is entirely decided by AdvanceRowColorPhase (below); this routine only outputs it at the right raster line.
headers.rom:EAD5: AdvanceRowColorPhase. Advances DrawGridScanlines' colour-phase source cells (ram_2290-22BC, ~44 of them, one per scanline) one step each: LDY ram_22xx / LDA ColorCycleSuccessor,Y / STA ram_22xx -- each cell's next value depends only on its current value, via the shared successor table at $FA4E. Each cell's update is individually gated by a bit test against a per-group table (dat_F7CD,X / dat_F804,X / etc., picked by shifting a distance-derived index and checking carry) before sub_F60D/sub_F44D's unrolled block touches it. That per-cell gating is the actual perspective-speed trick: rows update (i.e. visually scroll) at different rates depending on which gate table and bit apply to them, which is what makes far rows crawl and near rows race. Called from the per-frame geometry pass around $F900-$F998 (sub_F998's Y-indexed loop writes the edge table that DrawGridScanlines reads, then calls this once). ColorCycleSuccessor's actual content is decoded -- see rom:FA4E.
headers.rom:FA4E: ColorCycleSuccessor, decoded byte-for-byte (raw bytes + RGB via tools/palette.py's ntsc7800(), full listing in docs/color-cycle-table.txt). The $FA4E-$FB45 span (248 bytes, up to InitPokeySilence) is NOT one continuous lookup -- it's 9 short islands of real data (2-32 bytes each) separated by long unused zero runs; each caller's index range is constrained by construction to land on its own island, so the zero space in between is genuinely dead, never actually indexed. Every island but one is a simple symmetric luminance ramp at a fixed hue (e.g. $FA5E: C8,CA,C8,C8,C8,C6,C8,C4,C8 -- luma dipping to a low point and climbing back, hue held at green) -- a smooth colour 'breathe' up and down, which is what AdvanceRowColorPhase's self-referential successor walk actually produces frame to frame. The first island ($FA4E-$FA6D, 32 bytes) is the exception: it cycles through four different hues (C/D/E/F, i.e. green through yellow-green) as well as luma, not just one -- consistent with this specific one being the horizon's colour gradient DliHandler_Grid was already documented as producing, rather than a per-row corridor pulse.
headers.rom:97EE: TriggerMatchEnd. Reached from sub_97C6 ($97C6, called every frame from VEC_996F's chain at $99CC) via the ram_22C7-vs-ram_22C8 comparison, and directly from a second call site at $9B89 inside sub_9B36 (the per-goal handler, see rom:9B36). CONFIRMED: ram_22C7/ram_22C8 are score digits. THREE real causes (a third, corrected in below, was originally miscounted as dead code) -- confirmed in run-02.inp's two matches: frame 13843, HUD 0:00.0 (timer expiry) and frame 22613, HUD 1:10.0 -- time still on the clock -- ram_22C7 written to exactly $0A (10) at $9B98, matching the manual's 'first to 10 wins' shutout rule; and confirmed in run-03.inp at frame 18074, a sudden-death ending at 7-3 (see the bit-6 correction below). Two earlier passes in this document got the score-path's exact mechanism wrong in succession -- both corrected here rather than left standing: 'sub_97C6's check is what actually catches the score case' (disproved -- ram_2020 was nonzero at frame 22613, and sub_97C6's own gate requires it to be zero), then 'ram_2026 bit 6 gates the score case' (also disproved -- a full-match read-tap across BOTH of run-02's matches shows bit 6 never gets set even once in either one). The REAL mechanism, confirmed with a PC-filtered write-tap on the exact instruction (INC ram_004C at $9B85, sub_9B36's L_9B7E): ram_004C is a heavily-shared zero-page scratch cell, but sub_9B36 itself sets it moments earlier (at $9B6D) to a $FF sentinel specifically when the ones-digit BCD addition it just performed needed a carry into the tens digit -- i.e. exactly 'this goal pushed the score across a 10-boundary'. $9B85's INC then either leaves it nonzero (ordinary goal, BNE skips TriggerMatchEnd) or, if it was $FF, wraps it to exactly $00 (BNE not taken, falls through to TriggerMatchEnd unconditionally). CONFIRMED LIVE: at frame 22613, PC=$9B85 fires twice in the same frame (two calls to sub_9B36 that close together) -- first producing $FF (skipped), then $00 (falls through, TriggerMatchEnd fires) -- an exact match to this mechanism, and a clean, fully deterministic answer to 'the precise comparison that fires the instant the score crosses 10'. CORRECTED (was wrong): an earlier pass here said the ram_2026 bit-6 branch at L_9B7E 'wasn't observed to fire in either recorded match' and speculated it might be dead code. It isn't -- see the full trace on rom:9B36's own entry, confirmed live in run-03.inp at frame 18074: bit 6 is set by sub_97C6 whenever it catches the score momentarily tied (frame 17117 here, a 5-5 tie that had been sitting since 14825), and the very next goal by either side -- 956 frames later in this case -- ends the match immediately via this branch, at whatever score results, not necessarily 10. So there are three real trigger paths, not two: timer expiry (sub_97C6, scores differ), score reaches 10 (sub_9B36's carry-wrap), and sudden-death-after-a-tie (sub_9B36's bit-6 check, this correction). The timer-expiry case goes through sub_97C6 as documented: ram_2020 (rom:2020) is a per-digit timer-roll bitmask that's essentially always nonzero while the on-screen clock is actively ticking (confirmed live: exactly $00 only at frame 1/boot, frame 202/pre-match idle, and frame 6934 in run-01, right before its timer-expiry match end) and only settles to $00 once the timer stops changing -- which is exactly what lets sub_97C6's gate open at expiry. Sets EndSequenceTimer (ram_22E1) to $B4 (180) or $F0 (240), chosen by whether ram_2020 is zero at the moment TriggerMatchEnd's own body runs -- 'was some HUD digit still mid-roll when we decided to end the match', not winner-side or human/droid as an earlier guess had it. Also sets ram_22C3/22C4/22E5/22E8 to fixed values and ram_2026 to $08 (the self-latch, checked by rom:97C6's outer gate to prevent any re-trigger for the rest of the match), and forces the spin's speed -- see rom:D19C. Screenshots: docs/img/matchend-dualview.png, docs/img/matchend-spin.png.
headers.rom:2020: ram_2020. NOT winner-side or human/droid, an earlier guess now corrected with evidence -- see rom:982D and the correction on rom:97EE. It's a 4-bit bitmask (one bit per on-screen clock digit cell: ram_2022/2023/2024/2025) written every frame by sub_982D, set when a digit's internal roll-frame counter wraps this frame. CONFIRMED LIVE (run-01.inp, full 9089-frame match): near-continuously nonzero and actively toggling from shortly after match start (screenshots from the same recording show the HUD's tenths-of-a-second digit changing at the same ~6-frame/0.1s cadence as the fastest-toggling bit, docs/img/ship-lod-*.png happen to span this exact window) all the way to frame 6934, where it settles at exactly $00 right as the timer stops at match end -- the only three frames it reads $00 in the whole recording are frame 1 (boot), frame 202 (pre-match idle), and 6934. Read by sub_97C6 as part of its 'is it safe to check for match end' gate (rom:97C6) and by TriggerMatchEnd itself to pick the end-sequence duration.
headers.rom:982D: sub_982D. Runs every frame (called once from sub_97C6's chain at $99AC). Four independent digit-roll counters (ram_2022/2023/2024/2025, one per on-screen clock digit cell -- minutes, tens-of-seconds, ones-of-seconds, tenths, matching the HUD's 'M:SS.T' format) each count down through a 10-entry frame-pair table (dat_9770/dat_977A, shared with the HUD text-setup routine sub_9784) and wrap independently; a bit in ram_2020 (rom:2020) toggles for whichever digit wrapped this frame via the classic 6502 'decrement, BPL skip-else-ORA-bit-and-reset' idiom, once per digit. The two characters selected each call are written unconditionally into the corresponding HUD character cells (ram_2015/2016, 2018/2019, 201A/1B, 201D/1E) regardless of wrap, so this drives the actual displayed glyphs every frame, not just the bitmask.
headers.rom:97C6: sub_97C6. Called every frame via sub_99C2's gate (rom:99C2-area, `ram_2026 AND #$49 OR ram_2020`, skip if nonzero) -- so this only actually runs on the rare frame where no HUD clock digit is mid-roll AND neither the self-latch (ram_2026 bit 3) nor the tie flag (bit 6) is already set. Compares ram_22C7 vs ram_22C8 (the two score digits): if EQUAL, sets ram_2026 bit 6 (the 'scores currently tied' flag consumed by sub_9B36's L_9B89, see rom:9B36) and some cosmetic state (ram_22E8/22E5), then returns via sub_B033 -- does NOT reach TriggerMatchEnd. If they DIFFER, decrements ram_22DB,X (X = which side is behind) and falls through into TriggerMatchEnd unconditionally. CONFIRMED LIVE this is the timer-expiry match-end path (see rom:97EE) -- the outer ram_2020==0 gate is what actually withholds it until the clock stops ticking, not this comparison itself, which would otherwise fire on the very first frame after any goal broke a tie. CONFIRMED LIVE the tie branch itself also fires in real play (run-03.inp, frame 17117, catching a 5-5 tie) -- see the correction on rom:9B36 for what happens to bit 6 afterward; an earlier pass elsewhere in this file wrongly called that branch unobserved.
headers.rom:9B36:
sub_9B36. The per-goal handler (called from rom:9AD6 when a goal is scored). Selects the scoring side (X/Y via a #$10 comparison on the value passed in A), decrements ram_22DB,X and ram_22C9,X-related counters, then does BCD-style carry arithmetic adding ram_22C0 (the goal increment) into the scoring side's ones-digit. FULLY RESOLVED (two corrections deep): the carry check at $9B57-$9B6D computes (digit+increment)-11 and, if that's >= 0 (i.e. this goal pushes the digit to 11 or more, one past the display value that would read as exactly 10), stores literal $FF into ram_004C as a 'carry needed' sentinel -- otherwise it stores the (negative) comparison result, any non-$FF value. Then at L_9B7E ($9B85), 'INC ram_004C / BNE L_9B8C' falls through to TriggerMatchEnd (L_9B89) exactly when that increment wraps $FF to $00 -- i.e. exactly the goal that crosses the 10-boundary, and only that one. CONFIRMED LIVE two ways: run-02.inp frame 22613 shows ram_22C7 written to exactly $0A (10) by this same code at $9B98 (a separate, later write computing the actual displayed digit), and a PC-filtered write-tap on the $9B85 instruction itself shows it firing twice within that frame -- first producing $FF (an ordinary goal moments earlier, skipped), then $00 (this goal, falls through, TriggerMatchEnd fires). This retracts an earlier note here attributing the trigger to ram_2026 bit 6 (see rom:97EE) -- that branch exists in the code (L_9B7E's 'AND #$40/BNE L_9B89') but a full-match read-tap across both of run-02's matches shows bit 6 never actually gets set, so the ram_004C carry-sentinel path is the one that actually fires in real play.

FOLLOW-UP, from a user-supplied recording (run-03.inp) that reaches a tied score and continues past it: the combined score is a SHARED, ZERO-SUM POOL capped at 10, not two independent per-player counters -- confirmed by tracing the exact arithmetic and matching it against a live goal that moved the score from 5-5 to 7-3. The code at $9B57-$9B7D computes (mydigit+increment)-11, adds the OPPONENT's digit (ram_22C7,Y) to that, and only when the running total (mydigit+opponentdigit) is already at or past the cap does it (a) reduce ram_22C0 -- the increment actually applied to the scorer's own digit at $9B95/$9B9F below -- and (b) subtract the SAME increment from the opponent's digit at $9B7B. Algebraically: while mydigit+opponentdigit < 10, a goal simply adds the increment to the scorer, opponent untouched, exactly like two independent counters (matching everything observed in run-01/run-02, where the combined total never got tested against 10 before a match ended some other way). Once mydigit+opponentdigit == 10, every subsequent goal transfers points instead of creating them: new_mydigit = mydigit+increment, new_opponentdigit = opponentdigit-increment, so the total stays fixed at exactly 10 forever after -- confirmed both algebraically (four hand-worked cases, including the live 5,5,inc=2 -> 7,3 case) and by the live capture itself. This is what makes 'first to 10' actually mean 'first to control the whole 10-point pool, i.e. drive the opponent to exactly 0' rather than a race to an independent fixed threshold -- and it's why TriggerMatchEnd's score-based trigger (above) only ever needs to watch one side's digit for reaching 10, since reaching 10 and driving the opponent to 0 are the same event once the pool is exhausted.

SECOND CORRECTION, retracting the retraction above: ram_2026 bit 6 is NOT dead code -- it fires in real play, confirmed live in run-03.inp, and represents a genuine THIRD way a match can end, not covered by 'timer expiry' or 'score reaches 10'. Full sequence traced precisely: at frame 17117, ram_2020 (rom:2020) settles to $00 exactly as its own documentation describes (the rare 'HUD clock digit not mid-roll' window), sub_97C6 (rom:97C6) runs, finds the score tied (5-5, a tie that had persisted since frame 14825), and sets ram_2026 bit 6 (ORA #$40) instead of reaching TriggerMatchEnd itself. Bit 6 then sits set for 956 frames -- nothing clears it -- until the next goal at frame 18074 (a 2-point shot moving the score from 5-5 to 7-3 via the pool mechanic above). At that goal, ram_004C holds $FC at L_9B6D (NOT $FF -- the carry-wrap path above does not apply to this particular goal), so L_9B7E's OTHER check ('LDA ram_2026 / AND #$40 / BNE L_9B89') is what actually fires, jumping straight to TriggerMatchEnd -- CONFIRMED via a direct PC-tagged trace of the $9B85 instruction (silent) versus ram_2026 itself (drops from $40 to $08, TriggerMatchEnd's own self-latch overwrite, on the very same frame ram_22EA -- TriggerMatchEnd's entry marker -- gets written). So: 'the score was ever tied, and sub_97C6 happened to get a chance to notice' arms a sudden-death condition that the very next goal -- by either side, for any amount -- resolves immediately, at whatever score results (7-3 here, nowhere near 10). This retracts the earlier claim that bit 6 'never actually gets set' -- that was accurate for run-01/run-02 specifically (neither reached a tie that persisted into one of ram_2020's rare zero windows) but not a general fact about the mechanism. See the correction on rom:97EE and item 1/item 12 in docs/FINDINGS.md for the consequences -- an ending previously characterised as 'timer expiry with a non-decisive score' in the overtime writeup was actually this sudden-death path, not a plain timer expiry.

FOURTH ADDITION: the HUD timer-freeze mechanism, and what an ordinary (non-match-ending) goal actually does between the shot and play resuming. Every goal starts at sub_D520 (rom:D520), which detects the ball-vs-goalpost collision, computes the score increment into ram_22C0, and clears ram_2026 bit 7 while setting bit 5 in the same instruction. That single write is the ENTIRE cause of the HUD freeze widely reported by players and confirmed live this pass (run-03.inp frame 3307: the displayed clock holds at '2:47.4' for 312 frames -- about 5.2 seconds -- while the underlying MatchTimerLo/Hi counter keeps incrementing normally underneath, confirmed via scr:pixel(), not the raw bytes): bit 7 is the same 'match actively running' flag SteerTowardTarget (rom:D1DA) and the ball's own renderer (rom:BF35) are gated on, and with it clear, the whole per-frame dispatch (rom:99A2's 'BMI L_99AA' check) routes to sub_9A14 instead of the normal chain, which never reaches sub_982D (the HUD digit writer, rom:982D) at all -- not stuck, simply not called. Traced the full staged sequence live (PC-tagged writes to ram_2026 across the same goal): (1) frame 3305, sub_D520 clears bit7/sets bit5 ($80->$20); (2) frame 3306, THIS routine (sub_9B36, at $9B48's 'AND #$CF') clears bits 4/5 once it's processed the score, leaving ram_2026 at exactly $00; (3) frame 3426 (120 frames later), sub_9A14's own per-frame check (gated on ram_2108 -- the theme song's own stream-position register, going negative -- the SAME gate already confirmed elsewhere as the goal-shrink reseed's trigger, rom:9D18) sets bit 2 (the identical transient value sub_9929 uses at a genuine match start) and calls sub_9D18 -> sub_9D23, the full match/round reset -- CONFIRMED LIVE this really does reseed goal geometry and player/ball starting positions after an ordinary goal, not only at true match start, resolving what 'once per theme-song loop thereafter' on rom:9D18 was actually describing; (4) frame 3619 (193 frames after that), the SAME ram_2108 gate fires again and finally restores bit 7 ($00->$80, or here from whatever bit2 left it at), resets the ball's own orbit-physics vector (ram_00C0/00C3/00C6, the exact cells RotateOrbitVector/BallOrbitPhysics operate on, rom:DB46/rom:DA66) to a fixed ($00,$80,$01) starting state, and calls sub_9CD3 (the PRNG-ish source also used for the theme) and sub_B0E5. So an ordinary goal is not just a score increment -- it's a scaled-down version of the match-start sequence, paced by the theme song's own loop position rather than a fixed frame count (hence the freeze's real-world duration, ~5.2s here, isn't a round number), and the HUD clock visibly stalling for that whole window is a direct, mechanical side effect of the same flag gating all of it, not a separate deliberate 'pause the clock' feature.
headers.rom:9A70: EndSequenceCountdown: DEC EndSequenceTimer (ram_22E1); BNE skips ReturnToAttract. CORRECTED: this does not simply tick down once per frame for a flat 180/240-frame duration as first assumed -- it's only even reached once THREE outer gates all pass (rom:9A5A-area: ram_2026 bit 3 set, ram_22E7 nonzero, ram_2108 negative, ram_213A negative -- see rom:213A), so on any frame one of those isn't satisfied, the decrement is skipped entirely and the spin visually holds rather than advancing. CONFIRMED LIVE this actually happens: run-03.inp's EndSequenceTimer takes 299 real frames (18074-18373) to count down its 180-decrement span, not 180 -- consistent with the countdown pausing on some frames rather than a uniform one-per-frame rate. Roughly matches the ~3-4 second spin/celebration window observed live in an earlier, less precisely measured recording (timer hitting zero ~frame 6980, cleanup firing at frame 7173, see rom:9A75) -- that measurement is still in the right ballpark, just not exactly 180 elapsed frames.
headers.rom:9A75: ReturnToAttract -- MISNAMED, kept for continuity but not accurate: this does NOT unconditionally return to the attract demo, only to a SHARED dispatcher (VEC_996F, rom:996F) that decides live whether to keep playing or show the demo. Fires once EndSequenceCountdown reaches zero. Zeroes ram_22E7/22DB/22DC and both MatchTimerLo/Hi (ram_23B5/23B3) -- CONFIRMED LIVE it does NOT touch the score digits (ram_22C7/22C8), which is exactly why what happens next depends on the score -- calls sub_B11D (restarts the theme song via LoadThemeSong), and sets TaskVecLo/Hi back to $996F. CONFIRMED LIVE in run-01.inp (frame 7173, an 8-2 timer-expiry ending with nobody continuing to play): the game is visibly back on the Atari/Lucasfilm boot-logo sequence by frame ~7300. CONFIRMED LIVE in run-03.inp (frame 18373, a 7-3 timer-expiry ending where the recording keeps providing input): this exact code fires -- same PCs, same writes -- but the match instead resumes as what plays like overtime, still at 7-3, because VEC_996F's own MatchTimerHi check (see rom:996F) treats the freshly-zeroed timer as license to keep processing gameplay rather than fall into the demo, and the score was never touched. See rom:996F and rom:BA81 for the full mechanism -- 'attract' only actually happens once MatchTimerHi climbs past its threshold with nobody having kept the match alive in the meantime.
headers.rom:9800: RETRACTED 'OVERTIME text' claim, corrected tile identification. An earlier pass rendered this region with gfx.py's indirect-mode (256-character grid) at a large --lines value and read what looked like the literal text 'OVERTIME' and a digit set. That was a tooling artifact: these display-list entries are direct-mode (4-byte, no indirect bit), each only 1-7 bytes wide -- nowhere near enough for a text string in direct mode -- and the indirect-mode grid at a large line count reads 256 unrelated byte-columns per line, any of which can coincidentally resemble real content. Re-rendered with gfx.py's new --direct WIDTH flag (added this session specifically because of this mistake) at each fragment's real width and the zone's real 8-line height, every one of them ($9F1E, $A20A, $A51E, $A659, $A80A, $A85A, and the earlier-confirmed $8020/$8038/etc. set) shows a small diagonal wedge/staircase shape -- the same tile vocabulary as the confirmed corridor floor edges, not text and not obviously a dedicated sprite either. What's still solid: a real triangular ship silhouette IS visible rotating in the spin screenshots (docs/img/matchend-spin.png) -- that's a direct screenshot observation, independent of this byte-level mistake. Working theory, not confirmed: the silhouette is assembled from several of these small diagonal-wedge fragments arranged across adjacent zones (the same construction technique as the floor), rather than being one dedicated ship graphic -- consistent with the fragment shapes, but the actual arrangement wasn't verified. During the spin, extra display-list entries pointing into this region get appended to the *same* corridor zones that normally hold only the floor graphics (e.g. zone 8's list at $2514/$2518 gained $A80A/$A80E on top of its usual $18A7/$18BF). The selector that chooses which fragment to insert is traced end to end -- see RotationPhase (ram_22C1) and rom:D19C -- that part of the finding is unaffected by this correction.
headers.rom:D19C: AdvanceRotationPhase. ram_22C1,X (RotationPhase, one per player) is a self-paced 0-3 counter: DEC ram_22E2 first (a per-player reload/pacing timer), and only once that hits zero does '(prev + carry) AND 3' get stored back into RotationPhase. During idle/undirected play the reload comes from ram_22E3 via a computed path at $D1B9-$D1CB (compared against #$79, so it varies rather than being fixed) -- but see SteerTowardTarget (rom:D1DA) for the actual Rotosnap driver, which writes RotationPhase directly rather than through this reload path. CONFIRMED why the spin is fast: TriggerMatchEnd's own setup ($9800-$9827, see rom:97EE) hard-codes 'LDA #$01; STA ram_22E2' -- forcing the pacing reload to the fastest possible value (advance every frame) as part of firing, rather than leaving it at whatever variable value normal play was using. Direct code proof, no live capture needed for this part.
headers.rom:D1DA:
SteerTowardTarget -- CONFIRMED as Rotosnap's real driver (RotationPhase writer, matches the reported 'two quick 90-degree turns' behaviour). RESOLVED after three successive rounds of live verification; two earlier guesses about its gate and inputs were wrong and are corrected here rather than left standing. Gate: 'LDA #$07; BIT ram_2026; BEQ continue; RTS' -- CONFIRMED live this is simply 'the match is actively running' (bits 0-2 clear continuously from match start to match end, zero correlation with PossessionState's several catch/release pulses), not a per-player possession flag as first guessed -- SteerTowardTarget runs every frame of live play regardless of who holds the ball. Called only when EndSequenceTimer==0 (i.e. not during the match-end spin -- see sub_D14A, its only caller). Inputs: calls AngleToPhaseDelta (rom:D239) via sub_D1EC twice (Y=0, Y=1 -- one call per player), combining two 16-bit fields (weighted x4 and x3) read from a 'slot' array populated by sub_9DB7 (rom:9DB7) -- a previously entirely untraced writer, found by PC-tagging every write to these cells after the static disassembler came up with nothing (RotateOrbitVector, the obvious suspect, writes different cells entirely). CONFIRMED via address arithmetic against DistanceToBall's already-established ball-position addresses: SteerTowardTarget's Y=0/Y=1 calls read sub_9DB7's slots 1/2, which are 'this player vs. the ball' and 'the ball vs. the other player' respectively -- so each player's Rotosnap steering is driven by that player's own position relative to the ball, not a stored goal coordinate as an earlier guess assumed. That earlier guess was reasonable to make and reasonable to doubt: a live capture during a persistent-possession window showed all four input bytes cycling through their full range every single frame, which is real (this is the SAME rotating orbit-phase vector BallOrbitPhysics (rom:DA66) computes for the ball's hover, not a raw pixel distance) but looked inconsistent with clean goal-facing. CONFIRMED LIVE what actually happens: `RotationPhase` was tapped across a full persistent-possession window (run-01.inp, frame 2959 onward, spanning five separate catch/release cycles through frame 3900) and changes exactly ONCE, 14 frames after the catch, then holds rock-steady for the rest of the window despite the ball's orbit vector cycling every frame underneath it. The reconciliation: AngleToPhaseDelta reduces the weighted combination to one of only 8 coarse sectors (AND #$07) -- the ball's small hover-radius wobble doesn't cross a sector boundary once the ship has settled, so the *sector* stays stable even though the raw bytes feeding it don't. This is a complete, live-verified account of the mechanism and its stability; whether the settled sector specifically corresponds to 'the goal' geometrically (as opposed to some other stable reference implied by the same weighted comparison) wasn't independently checked against an on-screen goal position, but the observed behaviour -- snap within a couple of frames of catching, then hold steady regardless of ongoing ball wobble or repeated catch/release -- is an exact match for what was reported.

FOLLOW-UP, direct test against the now-confirmed real goal position (rom:9DD0's entities 9/10/18/19): NEGATIVE, and informative. Sampled the goalpost's on-screen X midpoint continuously through the exact frame RotationPhase settles (2973-2974 in run-01.inp) and periodically for 900 frames afterward while RotationPhase held constant. No settling toward centre ($80, the confirmed screen-centre reference from sub_9CF5's own arithmetic) is visible at all -- the midpoint sweeps through a wide range at a steady, roughly constant rate BOTH before and after the phase settles, passing through $80 once around frame 2960 purely in the middle of an uninterrupted linear drift, with no discontinuity when RotationPhase actually changes at 2973. So the goalpost's screen position is dominated by something continuous and apparently independent of RotationPhase (plausibly the corridor's own scroll/curvature, not yet identified) -- a confound that means this simple 'is it centred' test cannot detect Rotosnap's true target even if the target really is the goal geometrically. Genuinely unresolved: either the goal-facing claim needs a more controlled test (isolating Rotosnap's contribution from the corridor's own motion), or the correct geometric reference is one of sub_9E7A's other slot families (12/13, 18/19, 24/25, via sub_9EBB) not yet traced, rather than the entities checked here.

FOLLOW-UP, RESOLVED POSITIVE with the controlled test the previous note called for: rather than reading a screen coordinate (confounded by continuous corridor motion, as shown above), this replicates sub_D1EC/AngleToPhaseDelta's exact 6502 arithmetic externally (matched byte-for-byte -- feeding it the REAL ball data reproduces the game's own live delta=0 exactly, a working sanity check) and runs the identical formula on the goalpost-relative fields sub_9E7A already computes every frame at slot 12 (entities 18/19, the 'far' alternative, rom:9DD0) instead of the ball data SteerTowardTarget actually reads. CONFIRMED LIVE, twice, independently: at the exact frame RotationPhase transitions to a new value (frame 2974 in one persistent-possession window, frame 5724 in a completely separate one later in the same recording), the goal-12-fed shadow delta comes out to exactly 0 (aligned) at that same frame -- nonzero just before, in both cases. So Rotosnap's ball-based steering does converge on a direction that also faces the confirmed real goalpost position, not merely a stable but arbitrary sector as the negative test above (mis)implied; the earlier negative result was a limitation of testing raw screen position, not evidence against goal-facing. The alignment is a snap-and-hold match at the settle instant, not continuous tracking: sampled onward from frame 2974, the goal-12 delta drifted back to nonzero by frame 3865 as the ship kept moving and RotationPhase (already at delta=0 on the ball data) had no further reason to correct -- consistent with the ball-orbit vector being a reasonable, if imperfect, real-time proxy for true goal direction rather than the game tracking the goal explicitly.
headers.rom:D239: AngleToPhaseDelta. Takes a signed difference (computed by the caller into A, compared against ram_0050) and reduces it to an 8-way sector (AND #$07, with a couple of edge-case adjustments around sector 4 gated by ram_004F's sign) to index AngleToPhaseDelta's own table, dat_D266 ($00,$00,$01,$01,$00,$FF,$FF,$00 -- delta -1/0/+1 per sector). Adds that delta to RotationPhase, AND #$03, stores it back -- a one-step proportional nudge toward the target angle, not a snap-to-facing. If the delta is nonzero (not yet aligned) it also decrements ram_22E4. Because RotationPhase only has 4 states (90 degrees apart), being 180 degrees off takes exactly two nonzero-delta calls to correct -- matching the reported 'two quick successive 90-degree turns' when the ship starts out facing away from the goal.
headers.rom:D8EC: PossessionCheck -- the per-player possession/catch/contest logic, called once per player (Y=0, Y=1) EVERY FRAME via sub_D8DB from the main gameplay chain, re-evaluated from scratch each time (not a latched state machine). REVISED after a live capture of two full recorded matches (run-02.inp) -- an earlier note here read PossessionState=$FF as 'now possessing'; the capture shows it's actually a one-frame pulse almost every time, immediately reset by the top-of-function gate on the very next frame. The real per-frame logic: 'CMP #$02 / BPL' on ram_235B,Y (distance) -- if too far, unconditionally force PossessionState (ram_22C3,Y) = $01 and return, REGARDLESS of whatever it was the frame before. Only if close does it check ram_2026's bit 7 (CONFIRMED live to be a GLOBAL flag, not per-player -- both players' checks read the same address). If that bit is clear, ALSO force $01. So there is no dedicated 'release' instruction to find: possession is re-derived fresh every frame from (a) live distance and (b) this global timing window, and falls back to idle the instant either fails -- exactly why 'either player's fire press' can end it, since the check that matters is proximity + global window + whoever's fire is down at that exact moment, not a flag one player is holding that needs explicit clearing. Only past both gates does it look at PossessionState: not-yet-possessing (not negative) reads THIS PLAYER's own raw fire button, ram_0145,Y / ram_0146,Y (from INPT4/INPT5 via sub_BBDD -- confirmed live to be read in-match, not just pre-match menu handling as an earlier pass concluded from watching the wrong derived flag, ram_0143). Fire down -> PossessionState = $FF for this one frame (a catch pulse, sound and visual side-effects fire from it, but it reverts to $01 next frame unless distance/window hold AND fire is down again). Fire not down -> more position checks ($D924); on success, PossessionState = $00 -- CONFIRMED LIVE as the actual persistent state (seen holding for 500+ consecutive frames in the capture, versus $FF's single-frame lifetime) -- plus a miss/bounce sound cue (sub_B0BB). Already-possessing case (PossessionState negative on entry): $D90D plays a catch-adjacent sound cue (sub_B0C1) then sets ContestFlag ($FF) for BOTH the current player (ram_22D7,Y) and the other player (ram_22D9,X, X = Y EOR 1) -- read by ENTRY_Nmi's default DLI trampoline ($DF9C) and by sub_BE22, both purely for a colour-flash visual cue on the contested ball, not for transferring state. PossessionState <= 0 (either $00 or $FF) is what BallOrbitPhysics (rom:DA66) requires to run -- see there for the hover/wobble effect, and note $00, not $FF, is the state actually driving it most of the time.
headers.rom:DA66: BallOrbitPhysics. Gated by PossessionState (ram_22C3,Y) being <= 0 (checked by RotateOrbitVector's caller, sub_D9BC: 'DEX; BMI' on the loaded state). Computes a position difference against ram_2358,Y/ram_235B,Y (the same arrays SteerTowardTarget's angle math uses) and, via RotateOrbitVector, applies a small rotation to the ball's velocity/position each call -- CONFIRMED this is the actual 'ball hovers and wobbles in front of you' effect reported: a continuous 2D vector rotation keeping the ball orbiting near the ship rather than a static offset. Runs for both PossessionState values <= 0, but a live capture shows $00 is the one that actually persists (500+ consecutive frames observed) -- $FF is a one-frame catch pulse (see the revised note on rom:D8EC), so in practice this is almost always running under the $00 state, not $FF. See rom:D1DA -- SteerTowardTarget reads this exact ball-vs-player relationship (via sub_9DB7, rom:9DB7, entity index 2 confirmed as the ball) to drive Rotosnap, and the orbit's small hover radius is exactly why RotationPhase settles and holds steady rather than chasing the wobble frame to frame.
headers.rom:9929: sub_9929. Arms the main gameplay task vector (TaskVecLo/Hi = $997C, VEC_997C -- the per-frame gameplay dispatch DistanceToBall and others hang off), zeroes both scores and several HUD position cells, and sets ram_2026 = $04 (bit 2) -- CONFIRMED LIVE this is a transient 'match armed, not yet playing' phase marker: it reads $04 at frame 2511 in run-01.inp and has already changed to $80 (bits 0-2 clear, bit 7 set) by frame 2704, right when the HUD shows the match actually starting (00000 0:00.0 -> counting). Whatever clears bit 2 between those two frames wasn't traced this pass, but the transition is what opens SteerTowardTarget's gate (rom:D1DA) and PossessionCheck's window (rom:D8EC) for the whole rest of the match.
headers.rom:9DB7: sub_9DB7. RESOLVED -- this is the previously-untraced writer of SteerTowardTarget's inputs (rom:D1DA), found via a PC-tagged write-tap after the disassembler's static trace never located a writer for ram_2358/235B/2376/2379 at all (RotateOrbitVector, the obvious suspect, writes a completely different set of cells -- ram_00C0/00C3/00C6 -- not these). Calls sub_9DD0 (rom:9DD0) three times with different (X,Y) entity-index pairs and a 'slot' number in ram_004D: slot 0 = entities (0,1), slot 1 = entities (0,2), slot 2 = entities (2,1). Entities 0 and 1 are the two players (ram_008B,X/ram_00A6,X etc, already established); entity 2 is the BALL -- confirmed by address arithmetic, not guesswork: ram_008B+2=$008D, ram_00A6+2=$00A8, exactly the fixed ball-position addresses DistanceToBall (rom:DCBE) already established independently. So slots 1 and 2 are 'this player vs. the ball' and 'the ball vs. the other player' -- SteerTowardTarget's Y=0/Y=1 calls read slots 1/2 respectively (via the +1 offset baked into its field base addresses), meaning each player's Rotosnap steering is driven by THAT player's own delta to the ball, not a stored goal position. See rom:D1DA for how this reconciles with the reported clean goal-facing behaviour despite the ball's position being a continuously-rotating orbit vector, not a stable point, while held.
headers.rom:9DD0:
sub_9DD0. Computes position deltas between two entity indices (X, Y, per the caller) in two different representations (ram_00A6/00A9-based and ram_008B/008E-based -- likely two different scaled/axis views of the same 2D delta, given the 3x/4x weighting SteerTowardTarget later applies to them) and writes the result into a slot (selected by the caller via ram_004D, X, or Y depending on a sign comparison at $9E26/BMI) across seven parallel field arrays: ram_2339, ram_2357, ram_235A, ram_2375, ram_2378, ram_2393, ram_2396. RESOLVED (was open): also called from sub_9E7A (rom:9E7A) with entity indices 9, 10, 18 and 19 and slot numbers 6, 7, 12, 13, 18, 19, 24, 25 -- CONFIRMED LIVE these higher entities are the two goalposts, not a guess: a live tap on entities 9/10/18/19's stored X-position shows entity 9 and entity 18 always read an identical value (same for 10/19), and entity 10's value is entity 9's plus a constant $80 (128) at every single frame observed -- a fixed goalpost-width separation, both values shifting together and steadily as the ship approaches, exactly the signature of two posts of one goal scrolling past in a screen-relative coordinate (unlike the players/ball, which move independently). SteerTowardTarget only reads slots 1-2 (the player/ball comparisons from sub_9DB7, rom:9DB7), so it never sees this goalpost data -- see rom:BD80 for where the goalpost slots actually get consumed.

FOLLOW-UP -- one goal, not two: all ten JSR/JMP sub_9DD0 call sites in the traced 58.5% of the ROM are accounted for (sub_9DB7's three, sub_9E7A's four, sub_9EBB's three), and between them they only ever reference entity indices 0, 1, 2, 9, 10, 18 and 19 -- no other index appears anywhere. Entities 9/10 and 18/19 are the SAME goal (identical live values, confirmed above), just two viewing-angle representations, not two physically distinct goals. Combined with the confirmed shared, zero-sum 10-point score pool (rom:9B36) -- where scoring transfers points from the trailing side rather than crediting an independent counter -- this is consistent with Ballblazer having a single, shared goal both players compete over rather than each defending their own. Not provable from this alone (41.5% of the ROM is still untraced, so an undiscovered second goal referenced only from unreached code can't be fully ruled out), but no evidence for a second goal turned up anywhere this was checked.
headers.rom:FC43: BootSirenWait. RESOLVED -- retracts an earlier guess that dat_FE4A's copied bytes were '5 task jump-vector address pairs' (they don't decode as plausible ROM/RAM addresses -- $7F56, $2A00, etc). They aren't addresses at all. Waits for a vblank edge, sets CTRL=$48, then copies 10 bytes (dat_FE4A's 4 bytes immediately followed by dat_FE4E's first 6, an incidental boundary crossing between two otherwise-unrelated tables -- dat_FE4E is separately confirmed as DliHandler_Grid's per-channel AUDF sweep deltas) into TaskVecLo..ram_0049 via a straight LDX #$09/loop copy. Only the first two bytes are meaningful as a pair -- TaskVecLo=$56 (86) and TaskVecHi=$7F (127) -- and they're two SEQUENTIAL countdown seeds, not one 16-bit address: DliHandler_Grid ($FDB7, already documented) decrements TaskVecLo once per ~16-zone 'big tick' (matches its own ram_0065 AND #$0F wrap) while doing an AUDF1-4 siren sweep (using the copy's trailing 6-7 bytes, at ram_0043-0049, as the running frequency shadow, added to by dat_FE4E's deltas each tick -- so those bytes really do double-duty as both a seed value and a delta table). Once TaskVecLo reaches exactly 0, DliHandler_Grid switches to counting TaskVecHi down the same way; once THAT reaches exactly 0 it arms a fixed AUDCTL/AUDF1/AUDF3 wind-down and a 36-tick countdown in ram_0042, after which TaskVecLo gets one final decrement as an all-done sentinel. Two busy-waits gate the main boot thread on this: 'LDA TaskVecLo; BNE loop' (rom:FC59, waits for the 86-tick ramp) then 'LDA TaskVecHi; BPL loop' (rom:FC60, waits for TaskVecHi to go negative, i.e. its own countdown finishing) -- the 36-tick wind-down after that runs unsynchronized in the background while the rest of the boot logo sequence proceeds. CONFIRMED LIVE (cold boot, no recording needed): TaskVecLo counts down 1/frame from $56 at frame 248 to $00 at frame 333 (exactly 85 frames later, matching the seed); TaskVecHi then counts down from $7E to $00 at frame 460, wraps to $FF at frame 461; TaskVecLo itself wraps to $FF at frame 497 -- exactly 36 frames after 461, matching ram_0042's seeded wind-down value precisely. This is the Atari/Lucasfilm boot logo's whoosh/siren sound effect and its synchronization with the visual sequence, not a task-dispatch table of any kind.
headers.rom:9E7A:
sub_9E7A. Called every frame from the same per-frame chain as sub_9DB7 (rom:9DB7) -- right after it, in the loop at $D174 (part of sub_D158, SteerTowardTarget's sibling in the main gameplay dispatch, see rom:D1DA/rom:D14A). Branches on RotationPhase (player 0's own facing) to pick one of two entity pairs -- (9,10) or (18,19) -- and compares the player (entity 0) against each via sub_9DD0 (rom:9DD0), storing the results in slots 6/7 (near) or 12/13 (far). Entities 9/10/18/19 are CONFIRMED LIVE as the two goalposts (see rom:9DD0). Falls into sub_9EBB (rom:9EBB), which does player 1's mirror of the same computation. So this is the per-frame 'which goalpost, and how far is each player from it' calculation -- feeding sub_BD80's distance-to-screen-scale math (rom:BD80) for the goalpost's on-screen rendering, not SteerTowardTarget, which reads a completely different pair of slots (1/2, the ball comparisons from sub_9DB7).

The exact selection rule (traced fully, not just sampled): for RotationPhase==0, ALWAYS picks far (slot 12, entities 18/19), position-independent. For RotationPhase==2, ALWAYS picks near (slot 6, entities 9/10), also position-independent. For RotationPhase==1 or 3, it depends on ram_00A9 (player 0's own Y-position high byte, the same address DistanceToBall already established) compared against #$1B (27): far if >= 27, near if less -- almost certainly which half of the corridor's length the player currently occupies, picking whichever goalpost representation is more relevant to their current position as well as facing. CONFIRMED LIVE, independently: the two Rotosnap-alignment tests documented on rom:D1DA used RotationPhase==0 (far aligned) and RotationPhase==2 (near aligned) respectively -- exactly matching this derived rule with no exceptions.
headers.rom:9EBB: sub_9EBB. Player 1's mirror of sub_9E7A (rom:9E7A) -- same shape, gated on ram_22C2 instead of RotationPhase directly. CONFIRMED LIVE: ram_22C2 is a fixed constant ($02, set once at match reset and never rewritten in either recorded match), so the gate's branch always resolves the same way in practice -- only the near-boundary path runs, comparing entities 9/10 against entity 1 (player 1, hardcoded Y=1) into slots 18/19; the far-boundary path (entities 18/19 vs player 1, into slots 24/25) is real code but was never observed to execute. RESOLVED (was open, flagged as possibly a second goal): it isn't -- a PC-tagged read-tap on slots 18/19's field addresses shows the same sub_BD80 instructions (PC=$BD88 etc, already documented on rom:BD80) reading them, via the same dispatcher's dat_E422[1]=18 lookup (rom:E378) that selects player 1's near-goalpost slot. So slots 18/19 are player 1's own view of the identical single goalpost sub_9E7A computes for player 0 at slots 6/7, not a separate goal. CLOSED (the 'read by real code too' above was wrong): none of the PCs that read-tap logged against slots 24/25's fields ($FDBD, $FCBE, $FCBC, $236D, $2370, $2371) are genuine readers. Checked each: $FCBE/$FCBC is 'LDA ram_0066 / BNE L_FCBC' -- a tight boot-time busy-wait loop with no reference to these cells at all, executing enough times per frame that it coincidentally overlaps with unrelated MARIA hardware DMA reads elsewhere; $236D/$2370/$2371 and $FDBD sit inside display-list RAM/DLI-handler territory, the same class of shared-bus PC-misattribution artifact already documented for the ship investigation (PC=$2404 there). Slots 24/25 have no writer (ram_22C2's constancy) and, properly checked, no genuine CPU reader either -- entirely dead, not merely unobserved.
headers.rom:9CF5: sub_9CF5. CONFIRMED LIVE: the shrinking-goal mechanic. Called with X = a per-player goal counter (ram_22C9 for player 0, ram_22CA for player 1 -- see rom:9D23) and Y = which entity slot to write. Reads dat_9CE5,X ($40,$C0,$80,$60,$50,$48,$44,$40 -- 8 entries, matching the counter's cap at 7) and writes ($80 + dat_9CE5,X) into entity Y's low X-position and ($80 - dat_9CE5,X) into its high X-position -- i.e. the table entry is a half-width around a fixed centre, seeding the goal's two edges. CONFIRMED, and CORRECTED after a first pass got the timing wrong: the resulting on-screen edge separation, indexed directly by the goal counter with no offset, is $80 (128, full) for counts 0 and 1, exactly $00 (both edges coincide -- the goal is genuinely closed) at count 2, then climbs back without a clean floor -- 64, 96, 112, 120 for 3 through the capped value of 7, then back to a full 128 once capped (dat_9CE5[7] == dat_9CE5[0]). A live PC-tagged trace on the exact instruction that loads the counter (LDX ram_22C9 at $9D5A, inside sub_9D23) confirms X is used directly, unmodified -- an earlier pass here mis-timed a sampling probe (see the correction on rom:9D18) and concluded there was a one-step offset in the index; there is not, the table is used exactly as written. CONFIRMED LIVE, symmetric: a second recording (run-03.inp, multiple goals each side) with a PC-tagged trace on every dat_9CE5 read across the whole match shows player 1's counter (ram_22CA, feeding entity 9) cycling through all of X=0-7 and producing the identical sequence -- 128, 128, 0, 64, 96, 112, 120, 128 -- exactly matching player 0's curve at every step. One table, applied the same way to both players' own goals.
headers.rom:9D18: sub_9D18. Falls straight through into sub_9D23 (rom:9D23) -- not a separate call, a shared tail. Three paths reach it: sub_9929's own tail (true match start, JMP at $996C), a JSR at $9AE3 (rom:9AD9's block, part of the per-frame goal-check chain, gated on ram_2108's sign), and a JMP from bank/context $BC8F. CORRECTED after a first pass got the trigger wrong: the ram_2108 check at $9AD9 is NOT gated behind a goal having just happened -- it runs every frame this chain executes regardless, converging with the goal-detection path above it rather than being nested inside it. ram_2108 is the already-documented ThemeSongTick (rom:B233 area) stream-position register, going to $FF specifically when the 603-byte theme song hits its own terminating byte and loops (see rom:B6D2) -- CONFIRMED LIVE this is completely unrelated to goal timing: SongPtrHi never changes and ram_2108 climbs through a goal event (run-02.inp frame 2918) with no interruption or reset, reaching $FF at frame 3038 purely because that's when the ongoing theme's own loop cycle completes, ~900 frames after the previous loop point, not ~120 frames after the goal. So sub_9D18/sub_9D23 re-run once per theme-song loop, each time picking up whatever ram_22C9/ram_22CA (rom:9CF5) currently holds -- not once per goal. A player who scores twice within one song loop only sees the goal geometry catch up to both goals at the next loop point, not incrementally after each one. (An earlier note here claimed a clean 15-reads-to-13-goals-plus-2-starts correspondence in run-02.inp; given the mechanism is song-loop-gated rather than goal-gated, that count is not a reliable per-goal signature and shouldn't be read as one, even though it happened to come out close in that particular recording.)
headers.rom:996F: VEC_996F -- CONFIRMED LIVE: the 'overtime' mechanism, and the reason ReturnToAttract (rom:9A75) doesn't always mean what its name says. Checked/armed as the current task both at true boot and by ReturnToAttract; NOT the same task as VEC_997C (rom:997C-adjacent, armed only by sub_9929 at a genuine fresh match start). Its own gate: 'LDA MatchTimerHi / CMP #$04 / BCC continue-gameplay / JMP sub_BA81' -- while MatchTimerHi is below 4 (roughly the first ~17 seconds after whatever last zeroed it), it falls through into the SAME per-frame gameplay chain used during normal play (DistanceToBall, sub_9A14/sub_99C2, the TriggerMatchEnd check at sub_97C6, EndSequenceCountdown) rather than showing any demo. Only once MatchTimerHi reaches 4 with nothing having reset it in the meantime does it jump to sub_BA81 (rom:BA81), the real attract/demo entry. Since ReturnToAttract zeroes MatchTimerHi but never touches the score digits, a player who keeps playing after a non-decisive (timer-expiry, score not at 10) match end just keeps this gate open indefinitely, effectively continuing the SAME match at its existing score under a fresh ~17-second window each time -- what plays like 'overtime'. Confirmed live in run-03.inp: a match ends 7-3 by timer expiry at frame 18074, ReturnToAttract's own code fires in full at frame 18373 (see rom:9A75), and play resumes at 7-3 rather than falling to the title screen, because input kept arriving before MatchTimerHi could reach 4.
headers.rom:BA81: sub_BA81. The true attract/demo entry, reached only from VEC_996F (rom:996F) once MatchTimerHi has climbed to 4 with no match kept alive in the meantime. Picks two pseudo-random values via sub_9CD3 (already documented as a PRNG-ish source for the theme song) into ram_22CF/ram_22D0, then arms VEC_BAAD (rom:BAAD) as the active task -- the demo's own per-frame loop, which waits for a real player to start a match rather than immediately resetting anything.
headers.rom:BAAD: VEC_BAAD. The attract-mode demo loop armed by sub_BA81 (rom:BA81). Checks ram_0140/ram_0141 (raw input port state) and, once satisfied, calls sub_9929 (rom:9929, the TRUE fresh-match start -- zeroes scores, arms VEC_997C) -- this is the actual 'press fire to start a new match' handler, distinct from and later than VEC_996F's own gameplay-continuation branch. Scores and match state stay exactly as they were left until this fires, which is why a match that ends without a winner and is left alone long enough genuinely does return to a title/demo state with stale scores still sitting in RAM until a fresh sub_9929 call clears them.
headers.rom:213A: ram_213A. A second, independent one-shot sound-effect channel's own countdown, separate from ram_2107/2108's main theme -- consumed at $B4C6-$B516 (a small self-contained routine cycling through several POKEY register shadows, ram_2113-211B, based on ram_213A's own low 2 bits, then decrementing it each call) until it goes negative, matching the exact structural pattern already established for the theme song's own duration counter. Seeded by sub_B0FD (rom:B0FD, $3B) -- CONFIRMED LIVE this is only ever reached from sub_97C6's 'scores differ' tail (L_97E8), i.e. specifically the timer-expiry match-end path, never the score-reaches-10 or bit-6-sudden-death paths (see rom:9B36) -- so it functions as a 'final buzzer' sound cue tied to that one specific ending, and its sign is one of the gates EndSequenceCountdown checks before letting the spin sequence's own countdown begin (rom:9A70) -- ensuring that particular sound effect isn't cut off before ReturnToAttract fires. For the other two ending causes, nothing resets it at that moment, so its gate is effectively already satisfied from whatever ordinary gameplay sound last used the channel.
